88	---
89	
90	## 4. Sell-Side Disagreement Axes
91	
92	The real arguments the sell-side is having on ASML right now:
93	
94	1. **Capex-cycle trough timing:** Does the cycle trough in H2 2026 and re-accelerate in 2027, or is the digestion period deeper and longer (into 2027–2028) given memory oversupply and smartphone demand weakness? Bulls model a sharp V-shaped inflection; bears model a prolonged L-shaped digestion. This is the single largest source of 12-month price-target dispersion.
95	
96	2. **High-NA economics at scale:** Will High-NA cost-per-wafer clear the threshold where customers prefer it to multi-patterning DUV at volume? Bulls cite TSMC's public endorsement and Intel's production commitments. Bears note that High-NA tools are €350M+ each, early yield data is opaque, and multi-patterning DUV (using multiple cheaper tools) remains a credible alternative for all but the most leading-edge nodes.
97	
98	3. **China revenue durability:** Is 15–20% China revenue a stable floor under the current export-control framework, or will progressive rule-tightening (especially to DUV service/spare-parts) erode it further? The sell-side range on China's 2027 revenue contribution spans roughly 8–22% — a wide disagreement that drives meaningful valuation divergence.
99	
100	4. **TAM ceiling — real or expandable?** ASML's own LRP (Long-Range Plan) implies ~$28B advanced-logic equipment TAM at ~86% EUV penetration. Is this a hard ceiling (the stock is penetration-limited, not share-limited), or is the TAM itself expanding via: (a) 3D-DRAM and multi-layer NAND raising EUV intensity per wafer, (b) advanced packaging (HBM stacks, glass substrates, chiplets) requiring new litho steps, (c) geographic fab proliferation (US, Japan, Europe) adding new customer relationships? Bulls argue the TAM is dynamic; bears argue the LRP already captures it.
101	
102	5. **IBM (services) growth as the moat anchor:** Is Installed Base Management (IBM) a durable ~25% revenue floor that grows with the installed base regardless of cycle, or is it more exposed to cycle risk than consensus assumes (specifically: customer utilisation drops reduce upgrade spend; China service restrictions reduce the addressable installed base)? Bears who challenge the IBM floor are implicitly challenging the "earnings-floor" thesis that underpins the MEDIUM confidence anchor.
103	
104	---
105	
106	## 5. Failure Modes
107	
108	These are the thesis-breaking scenarios that the DCF does not capture because they are discrete rather than smooth:
109	
110	- **Customer concentration shock:** TSMC + Samsung + Intel represent the dominant share of EUV system revenue. [TODO: verify exact % against latest 20-F] A single customer deferrring a node by 12+ months or announcing a major capex freeze moves ASML's near-term revenue by a multiple of consensus expectations. This is not a gradual risk — it is a lumpy, concentrated exposure.
111	
112	- **China service/spare-parts export controls:** Current restrictions primarily cover new EUV and advanced DUV system sales. If rules extend to servicing or supplying spare parts to the existing DUV installed base in China, ASML's most cycle-resistant revenue stream is impaired. This would be the bear case's "earnings-floor-removal" event — the scenario where the business becomes more cyclical than the base case assumes.
113	
114	- **High-NA economics failure:** High-NA adoption depends on cost-per-wafer clearing the threshold where customers prefer it to multi-patterning DUV. If High-NA tool yields remain low, learning curves are steeper than expected, or customer process engineers can't close the cost equation, adoption slows. This breaks the post-2027 unit-volume and ASP expansion thesis simultaneously — the two largest contributors to LRP upper-bound revenue.
115	
116	- **Broad capex air-pocket (multi-segment, simultaneous):** The bear case is NOT "AI investment pauses." The more dangerous scenario is a broad-based semi downturn overlapping across memory (DRAM/NAND oversupply), mobile (smartphone unit weakness), and mature-node (industrial / auto demand normalisation) segments at once. In this scenario, even IBM service revenue is pressured by customer utilisation declines, and ASML's financial performance is worse than any single-segment stress model predicts.
117	
118	- **FCF distortion from customer prepayments:** ASML's reported FCF is significantly affected by customer prepayment timing. In strong-order years, prepayments boost FCF above earnings; in weak-order years, the reverse. Using any single-year TTM FCF as a DCF anchor without working-capital normalisation produces misleading base-year CAGRs. The `terminal_margin` override partially mitigates this by anchoring on a normalised steady-state rather than TTM, but the Y1 FCF used in the DCF can still be distorted.
119	
120	- **EUR/USD strengthening:** ASML reports in EUR. Persistent EUR appreciation against USD reduces translated revenue and EPS for US-listed ADR investors (ASML US), even with no change in the underlying business. Because the customer base (TSMC, Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) operates in USD-denominated capital markets, ASML's competitive position is unaffected by FX — but the P&L in USD terms is sensitive.
121	
122	---
123	
124	## 6. Ticker-Specific Overrides (Rationale)
125	
126	| Field | Value | Rationale |
127	|---|---|---|
128	| `base_wacc` | 8.5% | Euro 10y Bund ~3.0% + Beta ~1.15 × 5.5% ERP ≈ 9.3%; less ~0.8pp monopoly-durability discount (EUV is a single-supplier market with no credible near-term challenger — NIKON exited advanced EUV; Canon competes only at dry DUV). Rounds to 8.5%, defensible mid-range of sell-side (8.0–9.0%). Reports in EUR; risk-free rate is EUR-denominated. |
129	| `growth_ceiling` | 15% | Anchored as a **fallback ceiling, not an absolute cap** — consensus `eps_growth_5y` from `get_estimates` takes precedence per override hierarchy. Set at 0.15 = upper-LRP-bound (13%) + ~2pp headroom for: (a) AI-driven wafer-equivalent demand expansion, (b) advanced packaging litho TAM beyond pure leading-edge logic, (c) 3D-DRAM / memory complexity raising EUV intensity per wafer. Below the generic 18% fallback because the structural TAM-penetration situation (~86% of advanced-logic equipment TAM per ASML signal note) makes the central case TAM-expansion-bounded, not share-gain-bounded. |
130	| `terminal_margin` | 30% | **Subjective steady-state; bear/bull asymmetric per `scenario_axes`.** Base 30% assumes High-NA reaches mature unit economics and working-capital swings dampen over a full cycle. Bear scenario anchors to `scenario_axes.bear.terminal_margin: 0.24` (TTM-clean, the "High-NA stays expensive / utilisation weakens" case) rather than a symmetric −5pp delta. Bull scenario lifts `growth_ceiling` rather than `terminal_margin` — the bull upside in this name is more volume / demand driven than margin driven. |
131	| `confidence_anchor` | MEDIUM | TAM ceiling and High-NA economics are live, contested, and unresolved theses. Even with good MCP data quality, the IV range is irreducibly wide. Honest cap is MEDIUM until High-NA volume ramp validates the post-2027 unit-growth premise. |
132	
133	### `scenario_axes` design rationale
134	
135	Standard ±multiplier scenarios would produce symmetric bear/bull deltas from the base. ASML's thesis is structurally asymmetric:
136	
137	- **Bear downside** is bounded: terminal margin can't fall below observed TTM-clean levels (~24%) in a cyclical scenario — setting `bear.terminal_margin: 0.24` pins the bear case to that floor rather than extrapolating below it.
138	- **Bull upside** is growth-driven: the bull thesis is that the TAM itself is expanding (advanced packaging, 3D-DRAM, geographic fab proliferation) — setting `bull.growth_ceiling: 0.20` allows the bull-case DCF to capture this without being artificially compressed by the 15% base ceiling when consensus is absent.
139	
140	Unspecified scenario fields fall back to standard ±multiplier per the loader spec.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## 7. Historical Reset-and-Recover Priors
145	
146	| Episode | Drawdown (approx) | Catalyst | Recovery | Lesson |
147	|---|---|---|---|---|
148	| 2018–2019 memory downturn | ~−35% peak-to-trough | DRAM/NAND oversupply; Samsung and Micron capex freeze | ~14 months; recovery on 7nm EUV ramp visibility | Memory-cycle resets are severe but time-bounded; the next-node demand catalyst (here: 7nm EUV qualification) is the recovery trigger |
149	| 2022–2023 post-COVID demand reset + first China export controls | ~−45% peak-to-trough | Inventory digestion; initial US-NL-Japan EUV export-control announcement | ~12 months; recovered to prior highs on AI capex thesis | China-rule announcement created a sharp drawdown but AI infrastructure re-rating overwhelmed it within a year; the recovery speed was highest when the next demand catalyst was already visible |
150	| 2024 DUV-rule expansion | ~−25% local drawdown | US-NL expanded DUV export-control rules; near-term China revenue ceiling repriced | Partial recovery on pre-cutoff order pull-forward recognition | Export-control tightenings are now modelled by the market as episodic, not one-time; each rule change is priced, partially recovered, and held as a risk premium in the multiple rather than extrapolated linearly |
151	
152	[Note: episode magnitudes are approximate from general industry knowledge; verify exact drawdown % and dates against price history before citing numerically.]
153	
154	**Mean-reversion implication:** ASML resets recover faster when the next-node demand catalyst is clearly visible and near-term (e.g., a specific customer node ramp, a confirmed High-NA qualification). Resets during periods of demand uncertainty (2018–2019, mid-2024) take longer. The current cycle-trough environment has a visible catalyst (High-NA ramp, AI capex re-acceleration) but uncertain timing — which is exactly the asymmetry captured in the `confidence_anchor: MEDIUM` override.
155	
156	Bear scenarios that assume a permanent structural break (China service rules removing the IBM earnings floor, High-NA permanently failing to clear economics) are qualitatively different from cyclical reset scenarios. Historical recovery priors do not apply to structural-break scenarios — those require re-valuing the business at a lower steady-state, not modelling a timed recovery.
157

27	# GOOG Playbook
28	
29	**Coverage status:** ESTABLISHED · INCUMBENT  
30	**Thesis in one line:** AI-search-disruption debate + DOJ distribution-economics remedies + AI capex cost-permanence question — three structurally intertwined uncertainties that generic INCUMBENT/ESTABLISHED defaults cannot price.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 1. Business Architecture
35	
36	### Segment mix (approximate FY2025 basis)
37	
38	| Segment | Revenue share | Growth trajectory |
39	|---|---|---|
40	| Google Search & Other | ~57% | Low-to-mid single digits; AI disruption is the structural risk |
41	| YouTube Ads | ~11% | Mid-teens; subscription (YouTube Premium) adds a recurring layer |
42	| Google Network (AdSense / AdMob / DV360) | ~9% | Declining; programmatic ad-tech under AdTech regulatory scrutiny |
43	| Google Cloud (GCP + Workspace) | ~13% | ~28–30% YoY; becoming the second material earnings contributor |
44	| Google Other (Pixel, Play, Maps, subscriptions) | ~5% | Mid-single digits; hardware margins thin |
45	| Other Bets (Waymo, Verily, etc.) | ~1% | R&D-stage; not meaningful to near-term FCF |
46	
47	**Revenue driver mechanics:**
48	
49	1. **Search:** Paid clicks × CPC (Cost Per Click). Absolute quarterly Search CPM (Cost Per Thousand Impressions) and click volumes are not disclosed by Alphabet (noted as OQ6 gap in the engagement-KPI map) — revenue-per-search trend is inferred from total Search & Other revenue YoY, not directly observable. This limits the precision of monetisation-compression monitoring; the playbook does not attempt quarterly KPI tracking.
50	
51	2. **YouTube:** Primarily video ad auction (CPM-based); YouTube Premium subs add a lower-variance recurring line. Ad load and engagement trends are disclosed directionally but not with unit-economics granularity.
52	
53	3. **Cloud:** Committed GCP revenue backlog + Workspace seats. Backlog growth is disclosed quarterly; it is the leading indicator for Cloud revenue trajectory.
54	
55	4. **Other Bets:** Waymo is the only Other Bets asset with a plausible near-term monetisation path (robotaxi per-mile revenue, fleet licensing). Not material to DCF (Discounted Cash Flow) in the base case.
56	
57	### End-market exposure
58	
59	- **Digital advertising (~77% of revenue):** Cyclical sensitivity to global ad-spend budgets; secular tail risk from AI-interface displacement.
60	- **Enterprise cloud (~13% of revenue):** GCP + Workspace; less cyclical; differentiated through Gemini integration.
61	- **Hardware / consumer services (~5%):** Pixel, Google One, Maps API — limited operating leverage.
62	
63	---
64	
65	## 2. AI Investment Cycle Position
66	
67	Alphabet spent ~$91B in FY2025 capex, ~70% AI-attributed per public guidance. This depresses TTM clean FCF margin and creates a two-sided uncertainty that is structurally different from a normal capex cycle trough: the normalisation path depends on **which of two competing margin theses proves correct.**
68	
69	**Path A — cost-temporary (base case):**  
70	AI model efficiency improves on hardware and software curves (inference cost-per-query falls as TPUs scale and model compression matures). Capex-as-share-of-revenue mean-reverts post-2027 as the build phase completes. Monetisation density per AI-assisted query holds near current levels or improves (AI Overviews maintain ad slots; AI Mode monetises at comparable RPM (Revenue Per Mille) to standard Search). Terminal margin recovers toward 30% SBC-stripped FCF.
71	
72	**Path B — cost-permanent (bear-case terminal margin thesis):**  
73	AI serving costs do not decay with scale at the rate Path A assumes — either because competitive pressure forces continued reinvestment, or because each AI query is structurally more compute-intensive than a traditional lookup. Simultaneously, AI-style answering reduces click-through rates, compressing ad density and CPC. Revenue growth decelerates while cost stays elevated. Terminal margin stabilises in the low-20s. This is the basis for `scenario_axes.bear.terminal_margin: 0.22`.
74	
75	**Base-case choice:** The playbook picks Path A but does not assume the asymmetry away. The `terminal_margin` base of 30% reflects Path A prevailing. The bear `scenario_axes` captures Path B as a discrete scenario — not a symmetric delta from base — because interface displacement and cost-permanence cause joint compression of both growth and margin simultaneously, which a symmetric ±multiplier cannot represent.
76	
77	**AI-capex normalisation signal:** The evidence-gating condition for Path A is a sustained decline in capex/revenue ratio after FY2026, visible across two consecutive annual periods. A ratio that re-elevates above FY2025 levels by FY2028 would be evidence for Path B.
78

81	## 3. Active Catalysts
82	
83	| Catalyst | Probability | IV impact | Direction |
84	|---|---|---|---|
85	| DOJ Search remedies finalised (default-payment restrictions, Chrome leverage, or divestiture ordered) | ~35% material remedy by end-2027 | −10–20% | Strongly negative — distribution economics impaired |

95	
96	## 4. Sell-Side Disagreement Axes
97	
98	Organised by the **4-layer AI-disruption taxonomy** plus Cloud differentiation. Each axis names what distinguishes temporary noise from structural change.
99	
100	### (i) Interface disruption
101	
102	**The question:** Do AI assistants become the primary discovery and navigation layer, displacing Google Search as the first-place-I-ask interface for high-intent commercial queries?
103	
104	- **Bull:** AI Overviews and AI Mode keep users inside Google surfaces for the queries that generate ad revenue; "where do you start a purchase or research query" surveys remain Google-dominant. Competitors capture curiosity and informational queries, not commercial-intent ones.
105	- **Bear:** AI-native interfaces (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, in-OS assistants, browser-native AI) capture meaningful share of commercial-intent queries — the queries that actually produce CPC revenue. Users who stop clicking to Google for high-intent searches stop generating ad impressions entirely.
106	- **Noise vs. structural:** A single-quarter deceleration in Search revenue growth is noise — ad-cycle effects, macro, seasonality, and mix-shift within Search all produce this. Structural signal requires: monotonic commercial-intent query-share migration **sustained across ≥3 quarters**; "first-place-I-ask" data from third-party consumer panels showing a durable shift (not curiosity queries — specifically purchase-research, product-comparison, local-service-intent); revenue-per-search trend declining even in periods of macro-stable ad spend. All three together constitute structural signal; any one alone is insufficient.
107	
108	### (ii) Monetisation compression
109	
110	**The question:** Even at stable Search query share, does AI-style answering structurally compress revenue-per-search — via fewer ad slots per query, reduced click-through, or lower CPC?
111	
112	- **Bull:** AI Overviews maintain or improve revenue-per-search through better ad-intent matching; users who get AI answers and then click on ads are higher-intent buyers; blended RPM (Revenue Per Mille) holds or expands.
113	- **Bear:** AI summaries satisfy the user's need without a click; ad slot count per query falls as above-the-fold content becomes AI-generated; CPC compresses as advertiser competition for fewer slots declines.
114	- **Noise vs. structural:** Revenue-per-search trend over ≥2 quarters, filtered against macro ad-cycle movements by comparing to peer ad platforms (Meta, Snap, Pinterest) at the same periods. A revenue-per-search decline that tracks macro peers is cycle noise; one that diverges negatively from peers while the macro environment is stable is monetisation-compression signal. Absolute click volumes and CPM are not disclosed (OQ6 gap), so the observable proxy is total Search revenue growth rate relative to peer ad-platform growth rates.
115	
116	### (iii) Cost disruption
117	
118	**The question:** Does AI inference cost remain structurally elevated, preventing margin recovery even if Search revenue holds?
119	
120	- **Bull:** Inference cost-per-query declines on TPU hardware scaling and model-efficiency curves (distillation, quantisation, smaller purpose-built models); capex/revenue mean-reverts post-2027; operating leverage reasserts as fixed-cost build phase completes.
121	- **Bear:** AI serving cost is a permanent elevated line item — each AI query is computationally costlier than a keyword lookup by a structurally different order of magnitude; competitive pressure forces continued reinvestment to match quality; the cost-efficiency gains are real but are competed away in the form of better product rather than margin expansion.
122	- **Noise vs. structural:** Capex/revenue ratio trend post-FY2026 across two consecutive annual periods. A ratio that declines from FY2025 peak toward pre-AI levels (≤15% of revenue) is Path A signal. A ratio that stabilises above 18% of revenue through FY2028 is Path B signal. Gross-margin segmentation data (if and when disclosed at the Cloud or AI-products segment level) would be the most direct evidence but is not currently available.
123	
124	### (iv) Ecosystem and distribution displacement
125	
126	**The question:** Does regulatory and competitive erosion of Google's distribution advantages structurally weaken the default-placement economics that underpin Search market share?
127	
128	- **Bull:** Distribution moats hold: Chrome browser default-search leverage continues, Apple default-search-engine payment (~$18–20B/year, market estimate) survives legal scrutiny in modified form, Android OEM agreements sustain Google's first-call position. Regulatory remedies stay at the margins (conduct rules, not structural separation).
129	- **Bear:** DOJ remedies materially weaken default-placement economics — payments-for-default restricted or banned, Chrome divested or usage-gated, Android default-app leverage limited. Independent of which specific remedy is imposed: the structural question is whether Google's distribution advantages durably erode. An ecosystem-level erosion would move Search market share on a multi-year lag, not immediately — making it a slow-burn bear case, not a binary one.
130	- **Noise vs. structural:** Actual remedies imposed (with material appeals exhausted, not just initial rulings); third-party measurement of default-search-engine market share in the 12–24 months post-remedy implementation. Court rulings that are appealed and do not result in operational changes are procedural noise; operational changes to the Chrome default or the Apple TAC (Traffic Acquisition Cost) payment are structural signal.
131	
132	### (v) Cloud differentiation
133	
134	**The question:** Is GCP developing durable economic differentiation, or participating in a capital-intensive AI infrastructure cycle where margins normalise to mid-cycle hyperscaler economics?
135	
136	- **Bull:** TPU + Vertex AI + Gemini-on-Cloud create a stack-level differentiation that justifies sustained pricing power; enterprise customers building Gemini-powered workflows create switching-cost stickiness analogous to AWS-native application lock-in; GCP margin expands sustainably toward AWS/Azure levels (high-20s to low-30s).
137	- **Bear:** GCP participates in the AI capex cycle as a capacity provider, but without the enterprise-grade trust, developer ecosystem depth, or data-gravity advantages of AWS or Azure; margins normalise to mid-cycle hyperscaler economics (mid-teens); GCP is a strategic hedge for Alphabet but does not compensate for Search revenue risk.
138	- **Noise vs. structural:** GCP operating margin trajectory reported across ≥4 consecutive quarters at scale; pricing power signals from renewal rate commentary and enterprise customer-mix data (disclosed intermittently). GCP margins below 15% by FY2027 would weaken the base-case Cloud offset; margins expanding above 20% by FY2027 would strengthen the bull case.
139	
140	---
141	
142	## 5. Failure Modes
143	
144	These are the thesis-breaking scenarios that the DCF does not capture because they are discrete structural shifts rather than smooth-curve adjustments:
145	
146	- **Interface displacement (structural):** Multi-quarter monotonic migration of commercial-intent queries to AI-native interfaces — invalidates the base revenue growth assumption. This is the failure mode that does not have a historical analogue in Alphabet's operating history: prior Search challengers (Bing, Yahoo relaunch) did not change user behaviour at the interface layer; AI assistants potentially do. [interface layer]
147	
148	- **Monetisation compression (structural):** AI Overview and AI Mode rollout compresses revenue-per-search durably; ad density falls as AI summaries occupy above-the-fold positions; CPC declines as advertiser competition for fewer slots decreases. This failure mode can coexist with stable query volumes — making it harder to detect via search share data alone. [monetisation layer]
149	
150	- **Cost disruption (structural):** AI capex/revenue ratio stays elevated beyond FY2028 with no margin recovery. In conjunction with monetisation compression, this produces joint revenue-and-margin pressure — the scenario captured by `scenario_axes.bear` compressing both `growth_ceiling` and `terminal_margin` simultaneously. [cost layer]
151	
152	- **Distribution remedy:** DOJ remedies impair default-placement economics materially. The specific form matters less than the functional outcome: if Google cannot pay for or mandate default Search placement in Chrome, Android, and Apple Safari, the structural query-share floor is removed. Independent of any single ruling's outcome — the structural impairment of distribution economics is the failure condition, not the legal calendar. [ecosystem layer]
153	
154	- **Cloud commoditisation:** GCP margins fail to expand durably above mid-teens by FY2027. This eliminates the optionality embedded in the base case — the assumption that Cloud eventually becomes a material second earnings engine that partially offsets Search risk. If GCP remains a mid-margin business, the base case requires Search to sustain its current earnings contribution with no structural offset. [ecosystem layer]
155	
156	- **Geo-regulatory contagion:** EU DMA, India CCI, and other-jurisdiction remedies replicate the distribution-economics erosion pattern outside the US market. The US DOJ case creates a precedent and negotiating template; a coordinated multi-jurisdiction wave of structural remedies could impair non-US revenue streams that are not currently in the bear-case model. [ecosystem layer]

Less ~1.0pp moat-durability discount (dominant Search economics + Cloud share gains remain intact today). Plus ~0.3pp regulatory premium (active DOJ remedies + AdTech + EU DMA + jurisdictional contagion risk). Sits at META parity (9.0%) rather than ASML monopoly level (8.5%) — Search durability is a live contested thesis, unlike ASML's EUV monopoly which has no credible near-term challenger. |

Consensus `eps_growth_5y` takes precedence when populated; this override is the floor/ceiling for the fallback path only. |

TTM clean margin is depressed by the AI build cycle. 30% sits between Search-segment-implied margin and capex-blended group margin — a defensible mid-range under the cost-temporary path. Path B (cost-permanent) downside is held discretely in `scenario_axes.bear.terminal_margin: 0.22`, not absorbed into the base value. Without `scenario_axes`, a 30% base-case terminal margin would be overconfident; with it, the base stays clean and the structural asymmetry is priced in the bear DCF. |
167	| `confidence_anchor` | MEDIUM | The AI-disruption thesis spans four distinct structural questions (interface / monetisation / cost / ecosystem) that cannot be resolved from current financials. MCP data quality is adequate (4y FCF (Free Cash Flow), SBC, diluted shares present); LOW would be too pessimistic on data quality grounds. Structural-behavioural uncertainty is what caps confidence, not data availability. Below META's HIGH because META's central debate (regulatory) is discrete and binary; GOOG's central debate (interface displacement) is continuous, multi-modal, and decision-relevant in the base case, not just in tail scenarios. |

169	### `scenario_axes` design rationale
170	
171	Standard ±multiplier scenarios would produce symmetric bear/bull deltas from the base. GOOG's thesis is structurally asymmetric in a way that requires explicit overrides on both dimensions simultaneously:
172	
173	- **Bear case:** Interface displacement causes **joint** compression of growth ceiling (query share migrates) and terminal margin (monetisation compresses + costs stay elevated). A symmetric −5pp terminal-margin delta off 30% (i.e., 25%) understates the joint structural-break shape. `bear.growth_ceiling: 0.04` anchors below the symmetric multiplier because the bear case is not a cycle trough — it is an interface-layer shift where EPS growth converges toward low single digits. `bear.terminal_margin: 0.22` sits below the TTM-clean FCF margin to reflect the joint structural break, not a recoverable cycle compression.
174	
175	- **Bull case:** The bull thesis is monetisation-density improvement + Cloud acceleration. `bull.growth_ceiling: 0.18` matches the upper bound of pre-AI-discount consensus and allows the bull-case DCF to capture upside without being artificially compressed by the 13% fallback. `bull.terminal_margin: 0.32` is a modest above-base anchor for the scenario where Path A delivers cleanly and AI Overviews monetise at parity to current Search.

184	|---|---|---|---|---|
185	| 2022 ad recession + iOS privacy reset | ~−45% peak-to-trough | Macro ad-spend contraction; Apple ATT (App Tracking Transparency) headwinds to ad-targeting quality | ~12 months; recovery on ad-market rebound and YouTube brand-advertiser return | Cyclical ad recessions recover on macro normalisation; the underlying monetisation mechanics remained intact throughout |
186	| 2023 Bing + ChatGPT integration scare | ~−15% drawdown | Microsoft integrated GPT-4 into Bing; sell-side concern about Search displacement | ~6 months; recovered as Bing share gains remained marginal and Google announced Bard/Gemini roadmap | A credible competitive interface challenge caused a multiple de-rate, but was not sufficient to structurally impair query economics at the monetisation layer |
187	| 2024–2025 DOJ verdict + AI-Mode launch uncertainty | ~−20–25% drawdown (approximate) | DOJ liability finding in Search distribution case; uncertainty around AI Mode cannibalising Search RPM (Revenue Per Mille) | Partial recovery as AI Overviews maintained revenue-per-search in initial disclosed metrics | Regulatory headline risk creates an IV-expansion event; recovery pace correlated with whether monetisation metrics held in the quarters following the ruling |
188	
189	[Note: episode drawdown magnitudes and recovery durations are approximate; verify against price history before citing numerically.]
190	
191	**Mean-reversion implication:** Prior episodes where Google experienced sharp drawdowns and recovered shared a common structural condition: user behaviour at the **Search query layer remained intact**. Ad-cycle recessions compressed revenue per query temporarily; Bing integration scared the multiple but did not move query-source share durably; DOJ rulings de-rated the distribution-moat premium but did not change where users began high-intent searches.
192	
193	**Structural caveat:** These priors apply only when the query-origination behaviour is structurally stable. If Search query share migrates because users adopt AI assistants as their primary discovery layer — the interface-displacement failure mode — the historical mean-reversion priors do not apply. The recovery mechanism in prior episodes was mean-reverting ad economics, not mean-reverting user behaviour. Interface displacement would break the recovery mechanism itself: there is no historical precedent for Google recovering from durable query-origination share loss to a competing interface. The 2023 Bing episode is the closest analogue, and its resolution (Bing share gains marginalised) cannot be reliably extrapolated to a scenario where AI assistants are natively integrated at the OS, browser, and search-bar level at scale.

## Headline finding

The two files are structurally **the same** (frontmatter + 7 sections) and on most sections roughly **symmetric in quality**, but they diverge sharply on **one section** and have a few **smaller asymmetries** that each could borrow from the other.

ASML is 18.4K bytes / 157 lines. GOOG is 24.0K / 194 lines. The ~30% size delta is concentrated in Section 4 (Sell-Side Disagreement Axes), not spread evenly.

## Section-by-section parity

| Section | ASML | GOOG | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frontmatter narratives | Bull narrative enumerates 6 explicit vectors (i)–(vi); base/bear concise | All three narratives concise; structurally framed but no enumeration | ASML's bull narrative is more textured |
| Frontmatter failure_modes | 6 items, no taxonomy tags | 6 items, **each tagged** `[interface layer]` / `[monetisation layer]` etc. | GOOG has stronger reading discipline |

| §2 Cycle Position | "Cycle-trough/inflection" framing; **numerically bracketed** (TTM-clean 24% / base 30% / earnings 35%) | Explicit **Path A vs Path B** two-thesis frame; named **evidence-gating condition** ("capex/revenue ratio post-FY2026 over two annual periods") | GOOG is more *structurally* explicit (named paths, falsifiable test); ASML is more *numerically* anchored. Each could absorb the other's strength |

| §4 Sell-Side Disagreement Axes | 5 axes, **one paragraph each** describing the debate | 5 axes, **explicit sub-structure per axis**: *The question* / *Bull* / *Bear* / **Noise vs. structural** | **Biggest gap.** GOOG's "noise vs. structural signal" discipline is unique and load-bearing — it tells the reader what to ignore vs. what to act on |
| §5 Failure Modes | 6 modes, 1 paragraph each, anchored to section concepts | 6 modes, 1 paragraph each, **layer-tagged** mapping to §4 taxonomy | Roughly symmetric; GOOG's layer tags add navigation |
| §6 Overrides + scenario_axes rationale | 4 fields with rationale; scenario_axes design subsection | 4 fields with rationale; scenario_axes design subsection. **GOOG's `terminal_margin` rationale is less numerically anchored** ("between Search-segment-implied and capex-blended" — no numbers) than ASML's (24%/30%/35%) | Both good; ASML's WACC + terminal-margin numerics are tighter |
| §7 Historical Reset-and-Recover | 3 episodes table; mean-reversion + structural-break caveat | 3 episodes table; mean-reversion + structural-caveat | **Symmetric** |

## The quality-bar gaps, ranked

**To bring ASML up to GOOG's bar:**

1. **§4 Sell-Side Disagreement Axes — restructure to GOOG's Bull/Bear/Noise-vs-Structural sub-structure.** Single largest gap. GOOG's "noise vs. structural" line per axis (e.g., "a revenue-per-search decline that tracks macro peers is cycle noise; one that diverges negatively from peers while macro is stable is monetisation-compression signal") is the most valuable analytical discipline in either doc and is entirely absent from ASML.
2. **Layer-tag the failure modes.** ASML could tag with `[demand layer]` / `[margin layer]` / `[regulatory layer]` / `[FX layer]` — mirrors GOOG's pattern and aids cross-referencing.
3. **§2 — add an explicit named evidence-gating condition** for the "cycle has troughed" thesis (e.g., SEMI book-to-bill, EUV unit run-rate threshold). Currently implicit in the bear case description but unlabeled.

**To bring GOOG up to ASML's bar:**

1. **Bull narrative in frontmatter — enumerate upside vectors with explicit (i)–(vi) structure** the way ASML does. Currently a single paragraph; ASML's enumerated bull narrative gives readers discrete optionality vectors to track.
2. **§6 `terminal_margin` rationale — anchor numerically** the way ASML does (24% / 30% / 35% bracketing). Currently says "between Search-segment-implied and capex-blended" without numbers, where ASML names them.
3. **§2 — bracket the terminal-margin choice numerically** as ASML does (TTM-clean → base → earnings-implied). GOOG's Path A/B framing is structurally strong but doesn't give the reader the same three anchor points.

## Where the differences are *appropriate*, not gaps

These reflect genuine thesis differences and shouldn't be forced into parity:

- **scenario_axes single-axis (ASML) vs. dual-axis (GOOG)** — ASML's bear is genuinely an isolated margin compression; GOOG's bear is genuinely a joint growth+margin break. The differing structure is correct.
- **Cycle framing** — ASML is a *known capex cycle* (well-understood mechanics, debate is about timing). GOOG is a *first-of-its-kind interface-displacement question* (debate is about whether the cycle category even exists). The Path A/B framing serves GOOG specifically because that bifurcation is the question; it would be over-engineered for ASML.
- **GOOG's longer §4** is partly *because* it has more disagreement axes worth structuring; not all of ASML's 5 axes need full Bull/Bear/Noise framing (e.g., "TAM ceiling — real or expandable?" might be cleaner as 1 paragraph).

## My recommendation

If the goal is parity at the **highest** quality bar, the single highest-leverage change is to **rewrite ASML §4 in GOOG's Bull/Bear/Noise-vs-Structural structure** and **add layer tags to ASML failure modes**. That alone closes ~80% of the gap.

Then **port two ASML strengths back to GOOG**: enumerate the bull narrative's upside vectors, and add numerical anchor points to the §2 and §6 terminal-margin rationales.

After the markdown is reconciled, the HTML rendering will inherit the structure — so the markdown changes should be the source-of-truth pass before re-rendering.

25	# ASML Playbook
26	
27	**Coverage status:** ESTABLISHED · INFRASTRUCTURE  
28	**Thesis in one line:** EUV monopoly + High-NA ramp + China export-control overhang, with the semiconductor capex cycle as the dominant input.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## 1. Business Architecture
33	
34	### Segment mix (approximate FY2025 basis)
35	
36	| Segment | Revenue share | Growth trajectory |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| EUV systems (standard + High-NA) | ~50% | Cycle-dependent; High-NA ramp adds a step-up from 2026 |
39	| Advanced DUV (immersion) | ~25% | Mature; sensitive to logic node digestion pace |
40	| Mature DUV (dry, KrF, i-line) | ~10% | Stable; exposed to auto / industrial / mature-node capex |
41	| Installed Base Management (IBM) — services + upgrades | ~15% | Most defensive; ~25% of revenue; less cyclical than new tool orders |
42	
43	IBM (Installed Base Management) is the earnings-floor segment: service contracts and upgrades on the ~4,000-tool installed base continue regardless of new-system order cycles. It is the component most vulnerable to a China-service-rule tightening scenario (see Failure Modes).
44	
45	### Key revenue drivers
46	
47	1. **EUV unit shipments** — the volume metric for leading-edge logic. Consensus expects a step-up to ~90–100 units/year by 2027 from ~50–60 in 2024; below-60 for two consecutive years is a bearish inflection signal.
48	2. **High-NA EUV ramp** — ASP (Average Selling Price) per High-NA tool is ~€350M vs ~€200M for standard EUV. Even 5 additional High-NA units/year moves blended ASP materially. First customer is TSMC; Intel and Samsung are expected second/third.
49	3. **China revenue share** — ranged 20–49% of system revenue (2022–2023 peak) before export-control restrictions; tracking ~15–20% under current rules. Further rule tightening is the bear-case revenue risk; stabilisation at current levels is the base case.
50	4. **IBM attach rate** — services revenue as % of cumulative installed base value. Rising attach rate signals customer utilisation and confidence; falling attach rate (e.g., from China service restrictions) is the canary in the earnings-floor thesis.
51	
52	### End-market exposure
53	
54	- **Leading-edge logic (HPC/AI + smartphones):** TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry — drive EUV and High-NA demand
55	- **Memory (DRAM + NAND):** SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung Memory — drive EUV-for-DRAM and advanced-patterning demand
56	- **Mature logic / specialty:** auto, industrial, IoT via mature DUV (less cyclically exposed but not immune)
57	
58	Customer concentration: TSMC + Samsung + Intel represent the dominant share of EUV system revenue. [TODO: verify exact top-3/top-5 % against latest ASML 20-F / annual report risk-factor disclosure — do not cite a specific number without verification]
59	
60	---
61	
62	## 2. Capex-Cycle Position
63	
64	ASML is in a **cycle-trough / inflection** phase as of mid-2026. The 2024–2025 digestion period (customers pausing orders after COVID-era over-ordering of DUV tools) is expected to trough in 2026, with re-acceleration in 2027–2029 on two overlapping drivers:
65	
66	1. **AI-driven advanced-node demand:** TSMC N2/N2P, Samsung 2GAP, Intel 18A ramps require sustained EUV intensity. Hyperscaler custom-silicon fabs (Google, Meta, Amazon) are incremental new demand on top of smartphone-driven baseline.
67	2. **High-NA volume ramp:** First High-NA tools are being qualified at TSMC Arizona and Intel Ohio. If High-NA economics validate (cost-per-wafer clears vs multi-patterning DUV), the step-up in ASP per unit creates a revenue tailwind independent of unit-volume growth.
68	
69	**Normalised-margin thesis:** The `terminal_margin` override of 30% assumes High-NA reaches mature unit economics, customer utilisation normalises post-trough, and customer-prepayment working-capital swings dampen over a full cycle. TTM clean FCF (Free Cash Flow) margin (~24%) is trough-distorted by both the demand digestion period and ramp-related investment; anchoring the DCF on TTM understates steady-state. The 30% base sits between TTM clean FCF (~24%) and TTM earnings margin (~35%, implied by P/E 49.5 / P/S 17.18) — a defensible midpoint.
70	
71	**Bear case:** If High-NA economics fail to clear at scale OR if the semi cycle air-pocket is deeper than expected, utilisation stays weak and terminal margin compresses to TTM-clean levels. This is exactly what `scenario_axes.bear.terminal_margin: 0.24` captures — it anchors the bear terminal margin at the observed trough rather than at a symmetric ±delta from base.
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 3. Active Catalysts
76	
77	| Catalyst | Probability | IV impact | Direction |
78	|---|---|---|---|
79	| High-NA volume production milestone at TSMC (first 5+ unit run-rate quarter) | ~40% by end-2027 | +10–15% | Positive — validates post-2027 ASP and unit thesis |
80	| China export-control broadened to DUV service/spare-parts | ~25% | −15–20% | Strongly negative — removes earnings floor |
81	| TSMC Arizona N2 ramp goes to plan (capex not deferred) | ~55% | +5–8% | Positive — confirms leading-edge demand base |
82	| Intel 18A achieves volume yield (customer ramp on-track) | ~30% | +5–10% | Positive — adds a third High-NA anchor customer |
83	| Broad semi-capex freeze (memory + logic simultaneously) | ~20% | −20–30% | Strongly negative — all segments decelerate |
84	| Hyperscaler custom-silicon fab commitments (Google/Amazon/Meta) | ~35% by 2028 | +5–10% | Positive — incremental leading-edge demand |
85	| Rapidus (Japan) first production milestone | ~25% by 2027 | +3–5% | Positive — new geographic customer |
86	| Semi-cycle inflection confirmed by leading indicators (SEMI book-to-bill >1.2 for 2+ quarters) | ~50% by end-2026 | +8–12% | Positive — re-rates forward estimates |
87	
88	---
89	
90	## 4. Sell-Side Disagreement Axes
91	
92	The real arguments the sell-side is having on ASML right now:
93	
94	1. **Capex-cycle trough timing:** Does the cycle trough in H2 2026 and re-accelerate in 2027, or is the digestion period deeper and longer (into 2027–2028) given memory oversupply and smartphone demand weakness? Bulls model a sharp V-shaped inflection; bears model a prolonged L-shaped digestion. This is the single largest source of 12-month price-target dispersion.
95	
96	2. **High-NA economics at scale:** Will High-NA cost-per-wafer clear the threshold where customers prefer it to multi-patterning DUV at volume? Bulls cite TSMC's public endorsement and Intel's production commitments. Bears note that High-NA tools are €350M+ each, early yield data is opaque, and multi-patterning DUV (using multiple cheaper tools) remains a credible alternative for all but the most leading-edge nodes.
97	
98	3. **China revenue durability:** Is 15–20% China revenue a stable floor under the current export-control framework, or will progressive rule-tightening (especially to DUV service/spare-parts) erode it further? The sell-side range on China's 2027 revenue contribution spans roughly 8–22% — a wide disagreement that drives meaningful valuation divergence.
99	
100	4. **TAM ceiling — real or expandable?** ASML's own LRP (Long-Range Plan) implies ~$28B advanced-logic equipment TAM at ~86% EUV penetration. Is this a hard ceiling (the stock is penetration-limited, not share-limited), or is the TAM itself expanding via: (a) 3D-DRAM and multi-layer NAND raising EUV intensity per wafer, (b) advanced packaging (HBM stacks, glass substrates, chiplets) requiring new litho steps, (c) geographic fab proliferation (US, Japan, Europe) adding new customer relationships? Bulls argue the TAM is dynamic; bears argue the LRP already captures it.
101	
102	5. **IBM (services) growth as the moat anchor:** Is Installed Base Management (IBM) a durable ~25% revenue floor that grows with the installed base regardless of cycle, or is it more exposed to cycle risk than consensus assumes (specifically: customer utilisation drops reduce upgrade spend; China service restrictions reduce the addressable installed base)? Bears who challenge the IBM floor are implicitly challenging the "earnings-floor" thesis that underpins the MEDIUM confidence anchor.
103	
104	---
105	
106	## 5. Failure Modes
107	
108	These are the thesis-breaking scenarios that the DCF does not capture because they are discrete rather than smooth:
109	
110	- **Customer concentration shock:** TSMC + Samsung + Intel represent the dominant share of EUV system revenue. [TODO: verify exact % against latest 20-F] A single customer deferrring a node by 12+ months or announcing a major capex freeze moves ASML's near-term revenue by a multiple of consensus expectations. This is not a gradual risk — it is a lumpy, concentrated exposure.
111	
112	- **China service/spare-parts export controls:** Current restrictions primarily cover new EUV and advanced DUV system sales. If rules extend to servicing or supplying spare parts to the existing DUV installed base in China, ASML's most cycle-resistant revenue stream is impaired. This would be the bear case's "earnings-floor-removal" event — the scenario where the business becomes more cyclical than the base case assumes.
113	
114	- **High-NA economics failure:** High-NA adoption depends on cost-per-wafer clearing the threshold where customers prefer it to multi-patterning DUV. If High-NA tool yields remain low, learning curves are steeper than expected, or customer process engineers can't close the cost equation, adoption slows. This breaks the post-2027 unit-volume and ASP expansion thesis simultaneously — the two largest contributors to LRP upper-bound revenue.
115	
116	- **Broad capex air-pocket (multi-segment, simultaneous):** The bear case is NOT "AI investment pauses." The more dangerous scenario is a broad-based semi downturn overlapping across memory (DRAM/NAND oversupply), mobile (smartphone unit weakness), and mature-node (industrial / auto demand normalisation) segments at once. In this scenario, even IBM service revenue is pressured by customer utilisation declines, and ASML's financial performance is worse than any single-segment stress model predicts.
117	
118	- **FCF distortion from customer prepayments:** ASML's reported FCF is significantly affected by customer prepayment timing. In strong-order years, prepayments boost FCF above earnings; in weak-order years, the reverse. Using any single-year TTM FCF as a DCF anchor without working-capital normalisation produces misleading base-year CAGRs. The `terminal_margin` override partially mitigates this by anchoring on a normalised steady-state rather than TTM, but the Y1 FCF used in the DCF can still be distorted.
119	
120	- **EUR/USD strengthening:** ASML reports in EUR. Persistent EUR appreciation against USD reduces translated revenue and EPS for US-listed ADR investors (ASML US), even with no change in the underlying business. Because the customer base (TSMC, Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) operates in USD-denominated capital markets, ASML's competitive position is unaffected by FX — but the P&L in USD terms is sensitive.

34	## 1. Business Architecture

42	| Google Network (AdSense / AdMob / DV360) | ~9% | Declining; programmatic ad-tech under AdTech regulatory scrutiny |

61	- **Hardware / consumer services (~5%):** Pixel, Google One, Maps API — limited operating leverage.

65	## 2. AI Investment Cycle Position
66	
67	Alphabet spent ~$91B in FY2025 capex, ~70% AI-attributed per public guidance. This depresses TTM clean FCF margin and creates a two-sided uncertainty that is structurally different from a normal capex cycle trough: the normalisation path depends on **which of two competing margin theses proves correct.**
68	
69	**Path A — cost-temporary (base case):**  
70	AI model efficiency improves on hardware and software curves (inference cost-per-query falls as TPUs scale and model compression matures). Capex-as-share-of-revenue mean-reverts post-2027 as the build phase completes. Monetisation density per AI-assisted query holds near current levels or improves (AI Overviews maintain ad slots; AI Mode monetises at comparable RPM (Revenue Per Mille) to standard Search). Terminal margin recovers toward 30% SBC-stripped FCF.
71	
72	**Path B — cost-permanent (bear-case terminal margin thesis):**  
73	AI serving costs do not decay with scale at the rate Path A assumes — either because competitive pressure forces continued reinvestment, or because each AI query is structurally more compute-intensive than a traditional lookup. Simultaneously, AI-style answering reduces click-through rates, compressing ad density and CPC. Revenue growth decelerates while cost stays elevated. Terminal margin stabilises in the low-20s. This is the basis for `scenario_axes.bear.terminal_margin: 0.22`.

75	**Base-case choice:** The playbook picks Path A but does not assume the asymmetry away. The `terminal_margin` base of 30% reflects Path A prevailing. The bear `scenario_axes` captures Path B as a discrete scenario — not a symmetric delta from base — because interface displacement and cost-permanence cause joint compression of both growth and margin simultaneously, which a symmetric ±multiplier cannot represent.

77	**AI-capex normalisation signal:** The evidence-gating condition for Path A is a sustained decline in capex/revenue ratio after FY2026, visible across two consecutive annual periods. A ratio that re-elevates above FY2025 levels by FY2028 would be evidence for Path B.

96	## 4. Sell-Side Disagreement Axes
97	
98	Organised by the **4-layer AI-disruption taxonomy** plus Cloud differentiation. Each axis names what distinguishes temporary noise from structural change.
99	
100	### (i) Interface disruption
101	
102	**The question:** Do AI assistants become the primary discovery and navigation layer, displacing Google Search as the first-place-I-ask interface for high-intent commercial queries?
103	
104	- **Bull:** AI Overviews and AI Mode keep users inside Google surfaces for the queries that generate ad revenue; "where do you start a purchase or research query" surveys remain Google-dominant. Competitors capture curiosity and informational queries, not commercial-intent ones.
105	- **Bear:** AI-native interfaces (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, in-OS assistants, browser-native AI) capture meaningful share of commercial-intent queries — the queries that actually produce CPC revenue. Users who stop clicking to Google for high-intent searches stop generating ad impressions entirely.
106	- **Noise vs. structural:** A single-quarter deceleration in Search revenue growth is noise — ad-cycle effects, macro, seasonality, and mix-shift within Search all produce this. Structural signal requires: monotonic commercial-intent query-share migration **sustained across ≥3 quarters**; "first-place-I-ask" data from third-party consumer panels showing a durable shift (not curiosity queries — specifically purchase-research, product-comparison, local-service-intent); revenue-per-search trend declining even in periods of macro-stable ad spend. All three together constitute structural signal; any one alone is insufficient.
107	
108	### (ii) Monetisation compression
109	
110	**The question:** Even at stable Search query share, does AI-style answering structurally compress revenue-per-search — via fewer ad slots per query, reduced click-through, or lower CPC?
111	
112	- **Bull:** AI Overviews maintain or improve revenue-per-search through better ad-intent matching; users who get AI answers and then click on ads are higher-intent buyers; blended RPM (Revenue Per Mille) holds or expands.
113	- **Bear:** AI summaries satisfy the user's need without a click; ad slot count per query falls as above-the-fold content becomes AI-generated; CPC compresses as advertiser competition for fewer slots declines.
114	- **Noise vs. structural:** Revenue-per-search trend over ≥2 quarters, filtered against macro ad-cycle movements by comparing to peer ad platforms (Meta, Snap, Pinterest) at the same periods. A revenue-per-search decline that tracks macro peers is cycle noise; one that diverges negatively from peers while the macro environment is stable is monetisation-compression signal. Absolute click volumes and CPM are not disclosed (OQ6 gap), so the observable proxy is total Search revenue growth rate relative to peer ad-platform growth rates.
115	
116	### (iii) Cost disruption
117	
118	**The question:** Does AI inference cost remain structurally elevated, preventing margin recovery even if Search revenue holds?
119	
120	- **Bull:** Inference cost-per-query declines on TPU hardware scaling and model-efficiency curves (distillation, quantisation, smaller purpose-built models); capex/revenue mean-reverts post-2027; operating leverage reasserts as fixed-cost build phase completes.
121	- **Bear:** AI serving cost is a permanent elevated line item — each AI query is computationally costlier than a keyword lookup by a structurally different order of magnitude; competitive pressure forces continued reinvestment to match quality; the cost-efficiency gains are real but are competed away in the form of better product rather than margin expansion.
122	- **Noise vs. structural:** Capex/revenue ratio trend post-FY2026 across two consecutive annual periods. A ratio that declines from FY2025 peak toward pre-AI levels (≤15% of revenue) is Path A signal. A ratio that stabilises above 18% of revenue through FY2028 is Path B signal. Gross-margin segmentation data (if and when disclosed at the Cloud or AI-products segment level) would be the most direct evidence but is not currently available.
123	
124	### (iv) Ecosystem and distribution displacement
125	
126	**The question:** Does regulatory and competitive erosion of Google's distribution advantages structurally weaken the default-placement economics that underpin Search market share?
127	
128	- **Bull:** Distribution moats hold: Chrome browser default-search leverage continues, Apple default-search-engine payment (~$18–20B/year, market estimate) survives legal scrutiny in modified form, Android OEM agreements sustain Google's first-call position. Regulatory remedies stay at the margins (conduct rules, not structural separation).
129	- **Bear:** DOJ remedies materially weaken default-placement economics — payments-for-default restricted or banned, Chrome divested or usage-gated, Android default-app leverage limited. Independent of which specific remedy is imposed: the structural question is whether Google's distribution advantages durably erode. An ecosystem-level erosion would move Search market share on a multi-year lag, not immediately — making it a slow-burn bear case, not a binary one.
130	- **Noise vs. structural:** Actual remedies imposed (with material appeals exhausted, not just initial rulings); third-party measurement of default-search-engine market share in the 12–24 months post-remedy implementation. Court rulings that are appealed and do not result in operational changes are procedural noise; operational changes to the Chrome default or the Apple TAC (Traffic Acquisition Cost) payment are structural signal.
131	
132	### (v) Cloud differentiation
133	
134	**The question:** Is GCP developing durable economic differentiation, or participating in a capital-intensive AI infrastructure cycle where margins normalise to mid-cycle hyperscaler economics?
135	
136	- **Bull:** TPU + Vertex AI + Gemini-on-Cloud create a stack-level differentiation that justifies sustained pricing power; enterprise customers building Gemini-powered workflows create switching-cost stickiness analogous to AWS-native application lock-in; GCP margin expands sustainably toward AWS/Azure levels (high-20s to low-30s).
137	- **Bear:** GCP participates in the AI capex cycle as a capacity provider, but without the enterprise-grade trust, developer ecosystem depth, or data-gravity advantages of AWS or Azure; margins normalise to mid-cycle hyperscaler economics (mid-teens); GCP is a strategic hedge for Alphabet but does not compensate for Search revenue risk.
138	- **Noise vs. structural:** GCP operating margin trajectory reported across ≥4 consecutive quarters at scale; pricing power signals from renewal rate commentary and enterprise customer-mix data (disclosed intermittently). GCP margins below 15% by FY2027 would weaken the base-case Cloud offset; margins expanding above 20% by FY2027 would strengthen the bull case.

190	
191	**Mean-reversion implication:** Prior episodes where Google experienced sharp drawdowns and recovered shared a common structural condition: user behaviour at the **Search query layer remained intact**. Ad-cycle recessions compressed revenue per query temporarily; Bing integration scared the multiple but did not move query-source share durably; DOJ rulings de-rated the distribution-moat premium but did not change where users began high-intent searches.
192	
193	**Structural caveat:** These priors apply only when the query-origination behaviour is structurally stable. If Search query share migrates because users adopt AI assistants as their primary discovery layer — the interface-displacement failure mode — the historical mean-reversion priors do not apply. The recovery mechanism in prior episodes was mean-reverting ad economics, not mean-reverting user behaviour. Interface displacement would break the recovery mechanism itself: there is no historical precedent for Google recovering from durable query-origination share loss to a competing interface. The 2023 Bing episode is the closest analogue, and its resolution (Bing share gains marginalised) cannot be reliably extrapolated to a scenario where AI assistants are natively integrated at the OS, browser, and search-bar level at scale.
194

Search-segment-implied margin is structurally higher: Search & Other at ~57% of revenue is Alphabet's highest-margin segment, with implied margins above 35% plausible given disclosed Cloud and Other Bets operating losses offset against group operating income of ~28–30% (approximate; GAAP segment FCF margins are not separately reported — treat these as order-of-magnitude anchors, not precise figures). The 30% base sits between the normalised-FCF floor (~22–27%) and the Search-segment ceiling (~35%+) — a defensible midpoint under Path A.\n\n**AI-capex normalisation signal:** The evidence-gating condition for Path A is a sustained decline in capex/revenue ratio after FY2026, visible across two consecutive annual periods. A ratio that re-elevates above FY2025 levels by FY2028 would be evidence for Path B."
}

   - **CSS:** `.p-segment-chart` wrapper, color tokens per segment, legend below
   - **A11y:** `<svg role="img" aria-label="Revenue composition: Search 57%, Cloud 13%, …">`; table in source remains canonical
   - **Why:** GOOG §1 and ASML §1 both present segment mixes as tables; a visual thumbnail would anchor readers before deep-dive prose

2. **Bull-Bear-Noise comparison matrix (P19)**
   - **Detect:** Section heading `/disagreement|sell-side/` + structure with repeated `**Bull:**`, `**Bear:**`, `**Noise vs. Structural:**` triplets
   - **Markdown shape:** H3 per axis, then three bold-paragraph triplets
   - **HTML:** 3-column grid per axis: Bull cell | Bear cell | NVS cell, each with coloured left border (green/red/gray)
   - **CSS:** `.p-axis-grid`, `.p-axis-bull`, `.p-axis-bear`, `.p-axis-nvs` with `border-left: 4px`
   - **A11y:** Headings preserve outline; color is decorative (label text carries meaning)
   - **Why:** Both GOOG and ASML §4 already have this structure but render as prose cards (ASML) or nested H3+prose (GOOG); pattern would unify and visualise the triplet structure

3. **Layer-tag legend with colour swatches (P20)**
   - **Detect:** Failure-Modes section where items carry `[tag-name]` suffixes or ASML's existing `.fm-tag` positional tags
   - **Markdown shape:** Prose list items with trailing `[interface layer]`, `[cost layer]`, `[ecosystem layer]` tokens; pattern extracts unique tags and generates legend
   - **HTML:** Small horizontal legend bar above the FM section: `[interface] [monetisation] [cost] [ecosystem] ...` with inline colored badges
   - **CSS:** `.p-layer-legend`, `.p-layer-tag { display: inline-block; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 3px; font-size: 0.7em; }`, color per layer
   - **A11y:** Legend is plain text (no pseudo-content); used as a reference for the main section
   - **Why:** GOOG §5 embeds layer tags in prose; ASML §5 uses left-positioned `.fm-tag` elements with custom CSS; pattern would standardise and make the legend reusable

4. **Scenario-axes triangle or spider chart (P21)**
   - **Detect:** Section `/overrides|scenario/` + YAML or table structure with `bear`, `base`, `bull` rows and multiple dimension columns (e.g., growth, margin, confidence)
   - **Markdown shape:** Fenced code block with YAML or three-row table: `scenario | growth | margin | …`
   - **HTML:** Inline SVG triangle (equilateral, bear/base/bull at vertices) or radar/spider chart; data points plotted as dots or a shaded polygon
   - **CSS:** `.p-scenario-chart` wrapper, SVG `circle` + `path` elements, color tokens per scenario
   - **A11y:** `<svg role="img" aria-label="Scenario ranges: Bear growth 4%, margin 22%; Base growth 13%, margin 30%; Bull growth 18%, margin 32%">`
   - **Why:** Both playbooks currently list scenario overrides in table or grid cells (GOOG in frontmatter, ASML in custom cells); a visual "shape" of the scenario space would make trade-offs intuitive at a glance

5. **Catalyst timeline with IV impact bars (P22)**

   - **CSS:** `.p-catalyst-row`, `.p-catalyst-bar { background: var(--ok) | var(--danger); width: <IV impact>%; }`

# Playbook patterns P18–P24 — design spec

The seven patterns below extend `references/html-patterns.md` so every body section of an equity-research playbook gets a treatment instead of falling through to prose. P21 and P22 promote the inline custom CSS already present in `ASML.html` (`.axis-card` and `.fm` / `.fm-tag`) into the formal catalogue so GOOG and future tickers (META, NFLX, AMZN) inherit them. Every pattern uses shell tokens only (`var(--accent)`, `var(--ok)`, `var(--danger)`, `var(--warn)`, `var(--info)`, `var(--muted)`, plus their `-soft` companions) so dark mode and print stay working with no per-ticker overrides.

A note on detection priority: P18–P24 should sit **after** P17 in the catalogue and the existing first-match-wins ordering means they only fire when an earlier pattern hasn't already claimed the section. P4 (NFR table) is the closest existing competitor for P18 / P20 / P24 — its detection trigger is `Target | SLO | p95 | Latency | Throughput | Availability | Budget` headers, none of which appear in playbook tables, so the patterns never collide. P17 (risks table) is the competitor for P22 (failure modes) — P17 fires on a markdown table with `Risk | Severity | Mitigation` headers; playbook failure modes are a bullet list with `[layer]` suffixes, so they never collide. Document this precedence explicitly in each pattern's text.

---

## P18 — Segment-mix horizontal stack bar

**Detect.** H2 text matches `/business architecture|segment mix|revenue mix/i` AND its body contains a markdown table whose first column header matches `/^segment$/i` (case-insensitive, trimmed) AND second column header contains `share` OR `%` OR `mix`. Detection trips at the table level — the pattern wraps the table with the chart, not the entire section. If only one of the two columns matches, the table falls through to prose. Avoids false positives in any non-playbook table that happens to use a generic "Segment" header by requiring the second-column share/percent signal as a hard co-condition.

**Choice: 100%-stacked horizontal bar over donut.** Donuts hide the long tail (slices below ~5% become unreadable arcs), require external legend mapping, and are awkward to print. A 100%-stacked horizontal bar reads left-to-right at any width, preserves the source-table ordering as labelled segments inside the bar, and prints cleanly. The source table sits directly below the bar and acts as the legend — no separate legend chip-row needed.

**Markdown shape.** Matches GOOG.md lines 36–44 and ASML.md lines 34–42 as-written. Zero markdown changes.

**HTML.**

```html
<div class="p-segmix">
  <svg class="p-segmix-bar" viewBox="0 0 400 32" preserveAspectRatio="none"
       role="img" aria-label="Revenue mix: Google Search 57%, YouTube Ads 11%, ...">
    <g>
      <rect x="0"   y="0" width="228" height="32" fill="var(--accent)"/>
      <rect x="228" y="0" width="44"  height="32" fill="var(--info)"/>
      <rect x="272" y="0" width="36"  height="32" fill="var(--warn)"/>
      <rect x="308" y="0" width="52"  height="32" fill="var(--ok)"/>
      <rect x="360" y="0" width="20"  height="32" fill="var(--danger)"/>
      <rect x="380" y="0" width="4"   height="32" fill="var(--muted)"/>
    </g>
    <g class="p-segmix-labels">
      <text x="114" y="20" text-anchor="middle">Search 57%</text>
      <text x="250" y="20" text-anchor="middle">YT 11%</text>
      <!-- omit text on slices <8% — table below carries the label -->
    </g>
  </svg>
  <!-- the original markdown table goes here, unchanged -->
  <table class="p-segmix-table">…</table>
</div>
```

The viewBox is `0 0 400 32` — the renderer normalises each segment's share to a 0–400 px x-axis. Labels render only on slices ≥ 8% to avoid overlap; the table beneath always carries the full label set.

**CSS.**

```css
.p-segmix { margin: 16px 0 22px; }
.p-segmix-bar { display: block; width: 100%; height: 32px; border-radius: 6px;
  overflow: hidden; border: 1px solid var(--rule); background: var(--surface); }
.p-segmix-bar rect { stroke: var(--bg); stroke-width: 1; }
.p-segmix-labels text { font: 700 11px/1 "Inter", ui-sans-serif, sans-serif;
  fill: var(--bg); letter-spacing: 0.02em; }
.p-segmix-table { margin-top: 10px; }
```

Slice colour cycle: `--accent, --info, --warn, --ok, --danger, --muted` in that order — six tokens, enough for every playbook seen so far. Label fill uses `var(--bg)` so it inverts in dark mode (light text on dark slice fill, dark text on light slice fill).

**Accessibility.** `role="img"` with an `aria-label` that lists every segment and share. The source `<table>` is the canonical data — screen readers reading the table get the full picture regardless of the bar's rendering.

**When to use.** Playbook §1 with a Segment / Revenue share table.
**When not to use.** Tables with >8 segments (the bar becomes unreadable) — fall through to prose. Tables whose share column is a range like "5–10%" (the bar can't render a range) — fall through to prose. The detection rule already enforces a numeric share format, but the pattern implementation should defensively detect ranges and skip.

**Verification.** Open both GOOG.html and ASML.html: bar widths sum to 100% of container; slice colours follow the six-token cycle; table is fully visible below; dark mode inverts the label text contrast; print renders the bar at black-and-white-distinguishable shades (the six tokens have distinct luminance, so this works without further effort).

---

## P19 — Margin position-band strip

**Detect (strict, to avoid false positives).** H2 text matches `/(capex|AI investment) cycle|cycle position|normalised margin|investment cycle/i` AND a single paragraph within the section contains all three of:

1. A keyword phrase matching `/normalis(ed|ation)|anchor|floor|ceiling|midpoint|sits between|range from/i`;
2. At least two numeric anchors of the form `\d+(\.\d+)?\s*%` within the same paragraph;
3. The numeric anchors are within 250 characters of each other.

All three are required — keyword-only or numbers-only paragraphs fall through to prose. The strict trigger is the cost of avoiding false positives in DCF prose, which is dense with `%` figures that aren't position anchors. The renderer extracts the numeric anchors in source order and labels them by proximity-to-nearest-keyword: `floor → low end`, `ceiling → high end`, `base / anchor / midpoint → marked tick`, otherwise positional fallback (lowest = floor, highest = ceiling).

**Markdown shape.** Matches GOOG.md §2 "Normalised-margin anchors" paragraph and ASML.md §2 "Normalised-margin thesis" paragraph as-written. Zero markdown changes.

**HTML.** A horizontal strip with two endpoint labels and a marker tick:

```html
<figure class="p-band">
  <figcaption class="p-band-cap">Terminal margin anchors (SBC-stripped FCF basis)</figcaption>
  <div class="p-band-strip" role="img"
       aria-label="Range: floor 22–27%, base 30%, ceiling 35%+. Base sits at 30%.">
    <div class="p-band-track">
      <div class="p-band-fill" style="left:0%;width:100%"></div>
      <div class="p-band-tick" style="left:62%"><span>30%</span></div>
    </div>
    <div class="p-band-ends">
      <span class="p-band-low">22–27%<br><em>normalised-FCF floor</em></span>
      <span class="p-band-high">35%+<br><em>Search-segment ceiling</em></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</figure>
```

The renderer computes `left:` for the base tick as `(base - low) / (high - low) * 100%`. When the source paragraph carries explicit floor/ceiling/base labels (most playbooks do), those become the end-label `<em>` lines; otherwise the labels are omitted and the strip shows numbers only.

**CSS.**

```css
.p-band { margin: 20px 0 22px; max-width: 640px; }
.p-band-cap { font: 700 12px/1 "Inter", ui-sans-serif, sans-serif;
  letter-spacing: 0.06em; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--muted);
  margin-bottom: 12px; }
.p-band-strip { position: relative; padding: 12px 0 4px; }
.p-band-track { position: relative; height: 10px; border-radius: 5px;
  background: var(--rule-soft); border: 1px solid var(--rule); }
.p-band-fill { position: absolute; top: 0; bottom: 0;
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--danger-soft), var(--warn-soft), var(--ok-soft));
  border-radius: 5px; }
.p-band-tick { position: absolute; top: -6px; width: 2px; height: 22px;
  background: var(--accent); transform: translateX(-1px); }
.p-band-tick span { position: absolute; top: -22px; left: 50%;
  transform: translateX(-50%); font: 700 12px/1 ui-monospace, monospace;
  color: var(--accent); white-space: nowrap; background: var(--bg);
  padding: 0 4px; }
.p-band-ends { display: flex; justify-content: space-between;
  margin-top: 10px; font-size: 12.5px; color: var(--muted); }
.p-band-ends em { display: block; font-style: normal; color: var(--fg-soft);
  font-size: 12px; }
.p-band-low { text-align: left; } .p-band-high { text-align: right; }
```

Gradient track uses red-yellow-green soft tokens — the visual reading is "the band spans distress → comfort and the base tick is here". Works in dark mode because all four tokens (`--danger-soft`, `--warn-soft`, `--ok-soft`, `--accent`) have dark-mode companions in the skeleton.

**Accessibility.** `role="img"` with a full `aria-label`. The source paragraph stays in the DOM unchanged immediately after the figure — screen readers get the prose narrative.

**When to use.** A §2-style paragraph with explicit floor/base/ceiling language and two-or-more percentage anchors.
**When not to use.** A paragraph that just lists historical margins without a "between" or "anchor" framing — the strict trigger keeps these out. If the renderer can't extract three numeric anchors confidently, fall through to prose; don't render a strip with only two numbers (it's just a range bar with no story).

**Verification.** Tick position visually matches `(base - low) / (high - low)`; gradient renders in dark mode; the source paragraph still appears unchanged underneath; the `aria-label` reads the anchors in numeric order.

## P20 — Catalyst probability × IV-impact mini-bars

**Detect.** H2 matches `/catalysts?|near[- ]term catalysts?|upcoming catalysts/i` AND a markdown table whose header row contains all three of (case-insensitive): `catalyst`, `probability` (or `prob`), `IV impact` (or `impact`).

**Choice: inline mini-bars over scatter.** A scatter plot with 8 catalyst points loses point identity (labels overlap, hover doesn't work in static HTML), and either the labels become unreadable or the chart becomes a connect-the-dots puzzle. Inline mini-bars on each row preserve identity, keep the table as the primary structure, and scan top-to-bottom — the order in which the analyst wrote them. The renderer parses `~35%` as 35, `~15–25%` as the midpoint 20, into a 0–100 probability value and `±10–20%` as the absolute midpoint (15) signed by the direction column.

**Markdown shape.** Matches GOOG.md §3 and ASML.md §3 as-written. Zero markdown changes.

**HTML.** Standard `<table>` with `class="p-catalysts"` plus two additional virtual columns inserted (`<th class="p-cat-prob-bar">` and `<th class="p-cat-iv-bar">`) carrying the bars:

```html
<table class="p-catalysts">
  <thead><tr>
    <th>Catalyst</th><th>Probability</th><th></th>
    <th>IV impact</th><th></th><th>Direction</th>
  </tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>DOJ Search remedies finalised…</td>
      <td class="p-num">~35%</td>
      <td class="p-cat-bar-cell"><span class="p-cat-bar p-cat-bar-prob"
        style="--w:35%"></span></td>
      <td class="p-num">−10–20%</td>
      <td class="p-cat-bar-cell">
        <span class="p-cat-bar p-cat-bar-iv p-cat-bar-neg" style="--w:15%"></span>
      </td>
      <td><span class="p-cat-dir p-cat-dir-neg">↓ Negative</span></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

The IV-impact bar's width is the absolute midpoint of the range, capped at 30% for visual normalisation (anything >30% saturates the bar — and >30% IV swings are rare).

**CSS.**

```css
.p-catalysts td.p-num { font-family: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, monospace;
  text-align: right; white-space: nowrap; }
.p-catalysts .p-cat-bar-cell { width: 80px; padding: 8px; }
.p-cat-bar { display: block; height: 8px; width: var(--w); border-radius: 4px;
  min-width: 6px; }
.p-cat-bar-prob { background: var(--info); }
.p-cat-bar-iv.p-cat-bar-pos { background: var(--ok); }
.p-cat-bar-iv.p-cat-bar-neg { background: var(--danger); }
.p-cat-dir { font: 700 12px/1 "Inter", ui-sans-serif, sans-serif;
  letter-spacing: 0.04em; padding: 4px 8px; border-radius: 4px; white-space: nowrap; }
.p-cat-dir-pos { background: var(--ok-soft); color: var(--ok); }
.p-cat-dir-neg { background: var(--danger-soft); color: var(--danger); }
.p-cat-dir-mixed { background: var(--warn-soft); color: var(--warn); }
```

**Accessibility.** Real `<table>` with `<thead>` / `<tbody>`; the bar `<span>`s are decorative — the numeric cells next to them carry the meaning. `--w` via CSS custom property keeps the inline style minimal and parsable.

**When to use.** §3-style catalyst tables in any playbook.
**When not to use.** Catalyst tables without a Probability column (the bars are the point of the pattern) — fall through to P4 numeric-table treatment.

**Verification.** Bar widths visually match the percentage cells; direction pills use the correct token; probability bars are uniform colour; IV-impact bars carry the green/red sign.
